doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: Bluegrass and mandolin as an early foundation
summary: Bluegrass was the local style; Collins played mandolin as a child and sees bluegrass as improvisational.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Did that part of the country have an identifiable style of music that you were growing up with?

Outside of a lot of bluegrass, a lot of real traditional, country music, bluegrass, pretty eclectic really. A lot of jazz fans, a lot of Dixieland fans and everything, but if there was one, I would say it would be bluegrass probably.
Bluegrass has — you played probably, some bluegrass then.
Yeah, I sure did. I played when I was very small I played mandolin in a bluegrass sort of situation.
Did any of the music that you learned in that situation help you in the jazz world?

Oh, yes, quite a bit. I would say that bluegrass is really the jazz of that kind of music because so much of it is off the top of your head type thing. Bluegrass musicians really plays the same songs all the time for instance, you know, a lot of times, but a little bit different every time, just a little bit different.
So it leans towards improvisation quite a bit then.
Yeah, quite a bit, yeah. And a lot of technical things, a lot of fast, really fast tempos, and very good musicianship.
I’ve always looked at those mandolin players and wondered — it’s such a small, little area to deal with it seems like.
Oh, I know it. And they’re speeding bullets you know.
